part_title: Generative AI, Transformers, Diffusion and Multimodal Models Explained
review_basis: Reviewed original local AIF M03 slide-09 through slide-14 images in full, including transformer attention, diffusion noising, modalities, AI/ML/deep learning overlap and model family comparisons.

scenes.title: What is Generative AI (Gen-AI)?
scenes.narration: We have already learned that many machine-learning models predict a label or a number. Generative AI focuses on a different kind of output: producing new text, images, code, audio or other content based on patterns learned from data. Follow the four panels in this picture. In panel one, the user types a prompt: write a short explanation of cloud computing for beginners. A prompt is the input or instruction that guides the model. The arrow takes that request to the foundation model in panel two. A foundation model is a broadly trained model that can be adapted to many tasks, often through prompting or further training. The illustration shows documents, pictures and video as possible training data, but the exact training mix depends on the model. Pretraining is the major learning stage performed before the model is used in an application. Modern models often learn through self-supervised objectives, where some of the learning signal can be created from the data itself rather than requiring a person to label every example. During inference, the trained model produces the response shown in panel three. It is not searching a stored page and copying it exactly. It uses learned patterns to generate a sequence that fits the request. That explains both its flexibility and its limitations: a clear-looking sentence may still be inaccurate. The final panel lists applications such as drafting text, summarization, information extraction, image generation and conversational assistance. The same base model may support several tasks, but we must choose a model that supports the required input and output type. Consider the travel itinerary example along the bottom. A person asks for a custom plan, and the model proposes one. Before booking a train or hotel, verify actual schedules and prices; generated suggestions are not guaranteed facts. Question: do we need generative AI if all we want is to assign a complaint to one of three fixed departments? Usually not; a classifier or simpler rules may be more suitable. Choose the technology according to the output and reliability requirement.

scenes.title: Transformers and attention: conceptual overview
scenes.narration: This slide contains the foundation of many modern language models, but you do not need advanced mathematics to understand the idea. Start in the first column with the sentence, the cat sat on the mat. A transformer is a neural network architecture that processes a sequence, such as text, using a mechanism called attention. A token is a small unit of input, often a word or part of a word. Notice the arrows around cat and mat. These words matter to each other when determining the meaning of the sentence. Attention allows a model to weigh which other tokens are relevant when interpreting one token. Now move to the middle panel. Each token is converted into an embedding, a list of numbers representing information the network can work with. The attention block compares the tokens in the current context and produces an updated representation. The grid is a conceptual drawing, not actual attention weights we measured. On the right, two architecture styles are shown. An encoder-only transformer focuses on understanding a provided sequence and producing contextual representations useful for classification or search. A decoder-only transformer predicts tokens for generation. Its causal mask prevents the next-token prediction from looking at future tokens that have not been generated yet. Layers of self-attention and feed-forward computations repeat to build richer representations. At the bottom, distinguish training and inference. During training, computation on a known input sequence can be parallelized for many positions while respecting required masks. During text generation, a decoder predicts a token, adds it to the current sequence, then predicts the next. That is called autoregressive generation. A beginner analogy is reading a sentence and using its surrounding words to understand what bank means; a financial bank differs from the bank of a river. The surrounding words change the interpretation. The model does not reason exactly like a person, but context changes how it processes a token. Check your understanding: does attention mean the model always considers every token equally? No. It computes relevance under its architecture and masking rules, and different layers may use different patterns.

scenes.title: Diffusion Models (ex: Stable Diffusion)
scenes.narration: Let's switch from language to picture generation. The upper-left diagram begins with a clear image of a cat. Across the row, random noise is gradually added until the picture is difficult to recognize. Noise means random visual variation, like static on an old television. During training, a diffusion model learns patterns that help it predict or remove noise at different steps. The arrow in the center points to the process used during image generation. On the right, we start with random noise, and the trained model performs many steps that gradually produce a coherent image. A text prompt such as a cat with a computer can help guide those steps, although the particular model and setup determine what conditioning it supports. The image becomes clearer as the generation process progresses. Imagine a blurry television picture improving step by step; that is a helpful analogy, although a diffusion model is not simply revealing a photograph that was hidden under static. It is constructing a new image by applying learned patterns during the reverse process. The example on the lower left shows a cat beside a computer. The model can produce many possible images from similar prompts. It may misinterpret details, invent objects or reproduce biases seen in its training data. The lower-right decision cue asks when to consider diffusion models. They are useful for generating visual content when you want a new image guided by text or other conditions, rather than an exact copy of a real photograph. If a company needs to read the total on a scanned invoice, is image generation the right first tool? No. That task requires extraction or recognition, not creating a new picture. Diffusion models are one approach to generative AI, and transformer-based text models are another. Both create outputs, but their internal processes and typical use cases differ.

scenes.title: Multimodal foundation models
scenes.narration: Look at the left side of this diagram. One user supplies a text question, what is this animal, together with a photograph of a cat. The word modality means a type of information, such as text, image, audio or video. A multimodal model can work with more than one modality, but we must check which combinations the specific model supports. Follow the two input arrows into the large model in the middle. It can use the question and the image together to produce a text description, shown on the right as this is a cat. That is image understanding with a text answer. Some other models can generate speech, pictures or videos, which the dashed examples illustrate. The drawing is a menu of possible capabilities, not a promise that one model supports all of them. Read the four points on the far right: multiple input types, one or more output types, relationships across types, and richer applications. Imagine a student uploading a diagram of the water cycle and asking for a simple explanation. A capable vision-and-language model could use the picture and question together to create an explanation. Another application might take an audio question and produce spoken guidance. But an ordinary text-only model cannot directly examine image pixels unless an application converts the image into a representation it supports. Similarly, a model that accepts images and text may still output only text. This matters in service selection and exam questions: input support and output support are separate. Before sending personal photos or recordings, check privacy, consent and data-handling requirements. Our practice question is this: if the requirement is to upload a photo and receive its description, what combination do we need? Image input and text output. We do not necessarily need video generation or an audio model.

scenes.title: Comparing learning methods through everyday reasoning
scenes.narration: The four columns on this slide are a recap of concepts that are easy to confuse, so start on the left. Artificial intelligence is the broadest field. It includes systems that follow human-written rules as well as systems that learn from data. The traffic light example shows a rule such as if the signal is red, stop. That is an explicit decision procedure. The second column is machine learning, a subset of AI that learns patterns from examples. Here a collection of labeled dog pictures helps a model learn to recognize the dog category. Supervised learning is the name for training with examples that include correct labels. Other machine-learning methods do not use labels in the same way. The third column is deep learning, which uses multi-layer neural networks to learn complex patterns from data. The illustration shows recognition of a dog under different lighting or camera angles, a common image-processing task. The fourth is generative AI: a model creates a new image or piece of text based on learned patterns. Modern generative AI often uses deep learning, but these categories overlap rather than forming four unrelated technologies. Follow the shapes along the bottom: AI contains ML, which includes deep learning, while generative methods commonly overlap with deep learning. The categories are not four steps that every application must complete. Try three examples. A university website displays a fixed admission date from a database: ordinary programming may be enough. A model estimates whether a student will need extra tutoring from past learning data: that is a prediction problem that may use machine learning. A writing assistant produces a first draft of a scholarship essay: that is generative AI. This final task also needs human review because the draft may contain wrong or invented facts. The takeaway is to identify the requirement first. A rule-based solution, a classifier and a generative model may all be intelligent software, but they are not the same choice.

scenes.title: AI and ML terminology recap
scenes.narration: This final diagram gathers model family names that often appear in technology articles and exams. Do not try to memorize the acronyms before understanding the task. Begin with the left panel, language models. GPT is a family of generative pre-trained transformer models used for producing sequences such as language or code. The example asks it to write a thank-you email, and the output is drafted text. BERT, by contrast, is a transformer model designed to build contextual language representations, useful for understanding tasks such as classification and search. The words river bank and money bank show why context matters: the same word can mean different things. Now move to the middle. Sequential data is information whose order matters, such as spoken sound, words or sensor readings over time. A recurrent neural network, or RNN, processes a sequence and maintains information from previous steps. The X one through X four blocks illustrate that progression. WaveNet is an example of a neural architecture used for generating realistic audio waveforms, including speech applications. In the right panel, ResNet refers to a deep residual neural network architecture often used for image recognition. The stacked image layers suggest how it learns useful visual features. A GAN, or generative adversarial network, uses a generator and a discriminator during training. The generator produces candidate content, and the discriminator tries to distinguish generated from real examples, providing a learning signal. Finally, SVM and XGBoost are examples of established machine-learning algorithms that can be effective for classification or regression on appropriate data. SVM stands for support vector machine. XGBoost is a family of gradient-boosted decision-tree methods. The key is not to claim any of these is universally best. If you need to classify structured business records, a traditional model may perform well with lower cost. If you need to draft an email, a generative language model fits the output. If you need to recognize objects in images, a vision model is a candidate. Ask the same four questions every time: what input do I have, what output do I need, how will I evaluate accuracy, and what cost or privacy constraints apply? That practical decision framework is more important for an AI Practitioner than memorizing model marketing names.
